items.description_html:
RT Neelkanth Mishra
As expected, with the fiscal headwinds fading and monetary headwinds (falling credit growth till 1HFY26) becoming tailwinds (credit growth accelerating), GDP growth is surprising on the upside, and should help push up consensus trend-growth estimates to 7%-plus. That is, with a neutral fiscal and monetary policy, the economy should still register 7.5% growth.

In this light, I was shocked to see the ill-educated and egregiously wrong claims made by some that if the 'original' base of June-2025 quarter was used, growth in the June-2026 quarter would be much lower.

The new series introduced in Feb-2026 cleaned up the data and also significantly improved the methodology. For those who track this for a living (and I used to be one such till 45 days ago) - the downward revision in the base was known in March (see our note published on 1-Mar):
https://research.axiscapital.co.in/ResearchPortal/Download?E=bbebfkbdb

As our note acknowledged, the new series increased credibility of estimates of real output.

That claim is so obviously wrong that several logical rebuttals have already been made. But bad information tends to travel further than good information, and so it is important to reiterate and reinforce the argument.

That such claims got traction is itself surprising, given that easy-to-track and not-possible-to-fudge indicators of economic activity have been so robust. While June-quarter data was strong, that momentum has picked up:
- personal vehicle (cars, SUVs) dispatches grew 35% YoY in August despite just 9% growth in exports. Even two-wheeler growth is now >20% (though helped by strong exports).
- And if that was consumption, commercial vehicle dispatches grew >40%.
- tax collection growth has picked up meaningfully. This is as real as it gets.
- Credit growth continues to surprise on the upside (albeit on a low base). Last year most believed the then-weak credit growth was a demand problem, whereas we steadfastly stated it was a supply issue - it has for now been addressed.
- indicators of construction are robust.

Hopefully, now there will be fewer people asking "why private sector investment is weak," given that there is clear evidence of investments.

That said, there is still slack in the economy, as seen in weak real-wage growth. It may take several quarters of above-trend growth for that slack to tighten, and bring back sticky inflation pressures.

items.title: Moderna is up ~100% premarket after melanoma vaccine trial success. Short explainer on why stock moved 100%+ rather than 20% The vaccine is not a prev...
items.description_html:
Moderna is up ~100% premarket after melanoma vaccine trial success. Short explainer on why stock moved 100%+ rather than 20%

The vaccine is not a preventive vaccine like a COVID shot. It's made after patient already has cancer. Each dose is built individually for that patient from the mutations found in their own tumour — you sequence the tumour, find the mutated proteins unique to it ("neoantigens"), and make an mRNA shot that teaches the immune system to hunt cells carrying those specific mutations.

It's the first proof the idea works. Neoantigen vaccines have been a theoretical hope in oncology for years, but this is the first randomised Phase 3 trial designed to definitively prove the benefit.

If the mechanism is real, it's platform technology — the same pipeline could in principle be pointed at lung, kidney, bladder cancers. One analyst noted the results also read positively for the vaccine's ongoing studies in other cancer types. That optionality is what "holy grail" headlines are reaching for.

items.title: The ₹6 lakh crore that "vanished" from India's GDP It didn't vanish. SBI Research's new Ecowrap says the full ₹42 lakh crore revision got re-measure...
items.description_html:
The ₹6 lakh crore that "vanished" from India's GDP

It didn't vanish. SBI Research's new Ecowrap says the full ₹42 lakh crore revision got re-measured, not erased, and the math is simpler than the outrage.

What the report actually shows:

- Nominal GDP was cut ₹41.8 lakh crore across Q1 FY23 to Q2 FY26. That is 4.1% of GDP over those 14 quarters, not a hole in the economy.

- Real GDP over the same window was raised ₹372 lakh crore. Lower nominal with higher real means prices came off, not output. Same goods, lower prices.

- 95% of the cut sits in one bucket: Trade, Hotels, Transport and Communication, down ₹39 lakh crore. Finance, Insurance, Real Estate and Business Services moved the other way, up ₹13.6 lakh crore.

- The reason is method, not manipulation. The FY23 series measures the informal economy directly using ASUSE and PLFS survey data instead of proxies, so activity got re-sorted between sectors.

- Revisions are routine: 239 over 70 quarters since FY09, 134 up and 105 down, with no pattern by government.

Key takeaway: the "missing" number is a measurement upgrade, not a disappearing act. Focus on the logic, not the print.

Caveat: this is SBI's own rebuttal in a live, politically charged debate. Anyone who distrusts the base-year switch will read the same revision differently.

• Memory gets a near-term Astra boost but is late-cycle be selective. CXMT for China localization/share gain. SK hynix / Samsung / Kioxia only tactical if tightness holds.

• Analog is the best non-AI hedge STM, NXP, Renesas. Early-cycle recovery, inverse of memory.

• Risk of under-investing now > over-investing. TSMC capex $60-64bn, 2026 growth >40%. ABF undersupply + HBM4E BEOL complexity keep supply tight.

Stay where the AI money is actually being spent.

items.title: The Next Cycle Isn’t Just Chips JPM’s Sept 2026 Global Markets Outlook isn’t another “buy AI” note. It’s a map of the physical and local constra...
items.description_html:
The Next Cycle Isn’t Just Chips

JPM’s Sept 2026 Global Markets Outlook isn’t another “buy AI” note. It’s a map of the physical and local constraints that will actually decide the next investment cycle:

• Compute stays scarce - old-GPU rental rates remain sticky, hyperscalers keep raising capex, SPE order books are only just turning. If AI is existential, semi spend still has a long way to go.
• Power is the new staple - the bottleneck is electrons, not models. Grid capex is exploding, Asia is quietly re-rating nuclear, and Korea power-equipment backlogs are already screaming.
• Robotics goes exponential - China industrial robot volumes are re-accelerating. Humanoids are moving from R&D curiosity into industrial + logistics use-cases on a multi-year S-curve.
• Defense umbrella expands - mil-spend/GDP is rising across India, Korea, Japan, Taiwan. Korea export orders are inflecting; India production is scaling. This is multi-year, not a one-cycle trade.
• Asia localizes - markets with lower foreign trading share look more resilient if dollar/flows get ugly. Households still sit in property + deposits; onshore volumes have already structurally lifted.

The last cycle was software + cheap money.

The next one is compute, power, robots, defense, and domestic buyers.

items.title: RT Aditi Shrivastava: Swish's best kitchens push out 1,200 orders a day. A regular cloud kitchen manages 100-150. That density is what investors are p...
items.description_html:
RT Aditi Shrivastava
Swish's best kitchens push out 1,200 orders a day. A regular cloud kitchen manages 100-150.

That density is what investors are paying for. Swish has filed to raise Rs 224.54 crore in an extended Series B led by Bertelsmann India, valuing it at Rs 1,653 crore post-money - up over 30% from March.

From our deep dive on the economics: owning procurement, kitchens and delivery keeps food gross margins at 60-70%.

Swish says they turn profitable at an order value of Rs 220-225.

The hard part is next.

Fifty-five kitchens today, at least 250 planned in Bengaluru alone. Whether the economics hold beyond its densest micro-markets is the real test - Zepto Cafe shut nearly 200 kitchens late last year, and Swiggy closed Snacc within a year.

The full story:

https://www.thearcweb.com/article/swish-food-delivery-quick-commerce-swiggy-zomato-bistro-yf9TeN7cSW74uVU0

items.title: RT Aditi Shrivastava: 🚨🚨 4 out of 10 medicines on your prescription won't be there when you walk into a Bengaluru pharmacy. That's the problem P...
items.description_html:
RT Aditi Shrivastava
🚨🚨 4 out of 10 medicines on your prescription won't be there when you walk into a Bengaluru pharmacy.

That's the problem Plazza is actually solving. Not 10-minute delivery - availability.

A few numbers from our latest piece:
•⁠ ⁠20,000 orders a month, up from 2,000 in December
•⁠ ⁠Rs 700 average order value
•⁠ ⁠70% of business from chronic prescriptions

The model is unusual for quick commerce.

1. Its stores are real 24x7 licensed pharmacies that double as fulfilment centres, because Indian drug rules leave no other way.

2. And there is no procurement team: searches and orders train the system to stock each store three weeks ahead.

Founder Aman Priyadarshi started by testing the idea in his apartment complex's WhatsApp group in Bellandur, buying and delivering medicines himself.

Two years on: a $15 million Series A from Accel, Elevation and Nexus.

https://www.thearcweb.com/article/plazza-takes-an-early-shot-at-pharmacy-quick-commerce-dyvQ4RIHqVjtgEiI

items.title: #DPIAlert | SoftBank and Alpha Wave have monetised stakes worth about Rs 2,200 crore ($233 mn) through their latest sales. But the outcomes are sharpl...
items.description_html:
#DPIAlert | SoftBank and Alpha Wave have monetised stakes worth about Rs 2,200 crore ($233 mn) through their latest sales. But the outcomes are sharply different.

Meesho: SoftBank sold about 1.7% for Rs 1,650 crore. It did not participate in Meesho’s IPO OFS, making this its first reported cash-out from the company.

SoftBank first invested in Meesho in 2021, at a valuation of $2.1 billion. The company’s current market capitalisation stands at about $10 billion.

Broadly, the latest sale translates into an estimated return of at least 4-5x.

Its remaining stake of roughly 6.9% is worth about Rs 6,500 crore.

Pine Labs: Alpha Wave sold nearly its entire 3.1% stake for about Rs 550 crore. The firm did not sell shares in the IPO, making this its first major liquidity event in Pine Labs.

Alpha Wave invested in Pine Labs at the peak of the funding boom in 2022, at a valuation of $5 billion.

With its current market capitalisation hovering around $2 billion, the investment translates into a loss of about 50%.

items.description_html:
RT Aditi Shrivastava
🚨 Nine in ten of Sahi's new users are poached from other brokers.

That is the good news and the problem, in one number.

Dale Vaz's three-year-old broking platform added almost 28,000 active clients in July 2026 — among brokers tracked that month, only Groww added more. It has moved past PhonePe's Share Market.

It has proved traders will switch. It has not proved they will stay.

"There is definitely an opportunity in this space, and investors are open to trying new platforms. The challenge for Sahi would be to prove that this is not a leaky bucket. Retention is the key in this business," Kae Capital partner Sunitha Viswanathan told The Arc.

Acquiring a broking customer can cost Rs 10,000. Vaz says Sahi's payback is four to five months, and that traders on the platform for a year trade 50% more than in their first month.

Our story: https://www.thearcweb.com/article/sahi-dale-vaz-stocks-groww-zerodha-JvhwMSEL0109eyoX

items.title: RT Neelkanth Mishra: As expected, with the fiscal headwinds fading and monetary headwinds (falling credit growth till 1HFY26) becoming tailwinds (cred...
items.description_html:
RT Neelkanth Mishra
As expected, with the fiscal headwinds fading and monetary headwinds (falling credit growth till 1HFY26) becoming tailwinds (credit growth accelerating), GDP growth is surprising on the upside, and should help push up consensus trend-growth estimates to 7%-plus. That is, with a neutral fiscal and monetary policy, the economy should still register 7.5% growth.

In this light, I was shocked to see the ill-educated and egregiously wrong claims made by some that if the 'original' base of June-2025 quarter was used, growth in the June-2026 quarter would be much lower.

The new series introduced in Feb-2026 cleaned up the data and also significantly improved the methodology. For those who track this for a living (and I used to be one such till 45 days ago) - the downward revision in the base was known in March (see our note published on 1-Mar):
https://research.axiscapital.co.in/ResearchPortal/Download?E=bbebfkbdb

As our note acknowledged, the new series increased credibility of estimates of real output.

That claim is so obviously wrong that several logical rebuttals have already been made. But bad information tends to travel further than good information, and so it is important to reiterate and reinforce the argument.

That such claims got traction is itself surprising, given that easy-to-track and not-possible-to-fudge indicators of economic activity have been so robust. While June-quarter data was strong, that momentum has picked up:
- personal vehicle (cars, SUVs) dispatches grew 35% YoY in August despite just 9% growth in exports. Even two-wheeler growth is now >20% (though helped by strong exports).
- And if that was consumption, commercial vehicle dispatches grew >40%.
- tax collection growth has picked up meaningfully. This is as real as it gets.
- Credit growth continues to surprise on the upside (albeit on a low base). Last year most believed the then-weak credit growth was a demand problem, whereas we steadfastly stated it was a supply issue - it has for now been addressed.
- indicators of construction are robust.

Hopefully, now there will be fewer people asking "why private sector investment is weak," given that there is clear evidence of investments.

That said, there is still slack in the economy, as seen in weak real-wage growth. It may take several quarters of above-trend growth for that slack to tighten, and bring back sticky inflation pressures.

items.title: RT Aakrit Vaish: India AI startup ecosystem is starting to have a moment. August was busy. • At least 3 mega seed rounds coming together for research...
items.description_html:
RT Aakrit Vaish
India AI startup ecosystem is starting to have a moment.

August was busy.

• At least 3 mega seed rounds coming together for research-forward companies
• 2-3 teams/founders relocating back from major US labs to build in India
• Half a dozen+ Series A/B/C rounds at significant step-ups
• Multiple companies crossing $10M ARR — and some already breaking through $30M
• 3-4 corporates now actively investing with significant strategic interest
• A few local PE firms increasingly moving earlier to lead Series A/Bs

And a lot of these are for India first AI plays rather than simply US exports.

Great to see the momentum, and still early in the grand scheme of things.
